title: Early Signs and Symptoms of Pregnancy
content:
The most reliable early sign of pregnancy is a missed period, but pregnancy hormones — primarily rising human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), estrogen, and progesterone — begin affecting the body even before that becomes obvious, and can produce a range of other early symptoms.

Tender, swollen breasts are one of the earliest and most commonly reported changes, sometimes appearing within one to two weeks of conception, well before a missed period. Nipples may also become more sensitive or appear slightly darker. Fatigue is another very early and common symptom — many people describe feeling unusually exhausted even with adequate sleep, largely driven by the rapid rise in progesterone.

Nausea, sometimes with vomiting and commonly called "morning sickness" despite often occurring at any time of day, typically begins around four to six weeks into pregnancy (counted from the last menstrual period) and is thought to relate to rising hCG and estrogen levels. It affects a large proportion of pregnancies to some degree, ranging from mild queasiness to more significant nausea, though severity varies enormously between individuals and even between pregnancies in the same person.

Other commonly reported early symptoms include increased urination frequency (as the growing uterus and hormonal changes affect the bladder and kidneys), mild abdominal bloating or cramping (sometimes mistaken for an upcoming period), food aversions or unusual cravings, mood changes, and a heightened sense of smell. Light spotting can also occur around the time of implantation, roughly six to twelve days after conception, though any bleeding during pregnancy is generally worth mentioning to a clinician rather than assumed to be implantation bleeding.

It's worth being clear that these symptoms are individually nonspecific — fatigue, bloating, and mood changes are also common premenstrual symptoms, breast tenderness happens outside of pregnancy too, and some people experience very few pregnancy symptoms at all, especially early on. This overlap is exactly why a home pregnancy test (which detects hCG in urine) or a blood test is the reliable way to confirm pregnancy, rather than symptoms alone. Home tests are generally most accurate when taken after a missed period, though sensitive tests can sometimes detect pregnancy a few days earlier.

Once pregnancy is confirmed, early and regular prenatal care is strongly recommended, both to establish accurate dating (important for monitoring the pregnancy's progress) and to begin routine screening — including, relevantly, blood tests for hemoglobin and thyroid function, since both anemia and thyroid dysfunction are more common during pregnancy and can affect both the pregnant person and the developing fetus if unaddressed.

Symptoms that warrant prompt medical attention during a known or suspected pregnancy include heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, fever, or vomiting so severe it prevents keeping down fluids (a more extreme pattern than typical morning sickness, sometimes diagnosed as hyperemesis gravidarum). This is general educational information, not medical advice — a missed period with other early symptoms is a reasonable prompt to take a pregnancy test and contact a clinician, not a diagnosis in itself.
